clue.text: Line taken from piece of traditional flooring 90 degrees apart

indicators.note: something taken from a whole is removed, so the railway letters are struck out of the flooring phrase

blocks.note: a quarry tile is an unglazed clay floor tile of the traditional kind
RY, railway, is the usual crossword abbreviation for a line

explanation.surface: A line has been lifted out of an old tiled floor whose pieces sit at right angles.
explanation.walkthrough: QUARRY TILE loses RY to leave QUARTILE.
explanation.definitionFit: In astrology a quartile aspect is the position of two planets separated by a quarter of the zodiac circle.

clue.text: First parent (either)

blocks.note: A is the first letter, as in A1 or grade A
a dam is a mother, especially of an animal

explanation.walkthrough: '(either)' says the phrase can be read either way: as A plus DAM, a first mother, or as the name of the first father in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible story Adam is the original man, father of the whole human race alongside Eve.

clue.text: Point to Mr Clarke as being socially pretentious

blocks.note: S, south, is a compass point
Nobby is the traditional nickname for anyone called Clark or Clarke

explanation.surface: Someone singles out a Mr Clarke and accuses him of putting on airs.
explanation.walkthrough: British nickname lore pairs surnames with set nicknames: every Clark is Nobby, as every Miller is Dusty.
explanation.definitionFit: A snob looks down on those of lower status, so snobby behaviour is affected social superiority.

clue.text: Puzzle (Araucaria's), with pen provided inside

indicators.note: the word for provided goes inside the word for pen, which wraps round it

blocks.note: the setter speaking of himself: Araucaria's is 'my'
a sty is a pen for pigs
provided that means if

explanation.surface: The setter introduces his own puzzle, which comes with a pen thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: MY then ST(IF)Y. A setter's name in a clue usually stands for ME, I or MY.
explanation.definitionFit: To puzzle someone is to bewilder or baffle them, which is what mystify means as a verb.

clue.text: Actors do the dirty on one: they were deprived for the sake of 17

definitions.text: they were deprived for the sake of 17

blocks.note: the cast is the set of actors in a show
to rat on someone is to betray them
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Some actors betray a colleague, before a grim aside about people who lost out for the sake of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 is SINGING. Boys were castrated so their voices stayed high, which is the deprivation the definition delicately hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: Castrati were male singers gelded before puberty to preserve a soprano or alto voice for opera and church music.

clue.text: Effect of slight stroke disconcerting in pool game

indicators.note: disconcerting means throwing into disorder, so the following letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ten letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A gentle cue stroke at pool has an unsettling effect on the play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stroke' looks like a shot at pool; here it is a mild stroke of the brain.
explanation.definitionFit: Monoplegia is paralysis of a single limb, which a minor cerebral stroke can leave behind.

clue.text: Wheeler-dealer's ending during the short days

indicators.note: an ending is the tail of a word, so only the closing letters of dealer are wanted
something happening during a period sits within it, so these letters go inside the days

blocks.note: the final two letters of dealer
Fri is the short form of Friday, so the days shortened are Fris

explanation.surface: A wheeler-dealer's career comes to an end in the dark days of winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wheeler-dealer' looks like one word, but the hyphen splits it: the wheeler is the definition and dealer only supplies its ending.
explanation.definitionFit: George Ferris built the first big observation wheel, for the 1893 Chicago fair, so Ferris is the original wheel maker.

clue.text: See 26
Sailor, name of Arup, in 22 across?

blocks.note: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor
Ove Arup was the Anglo-Danish engineer behind the Sydney Opera House structure

explanation.surface: A sailor and the engineer Arup are imagined up in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 across is HEAVEN, and what is in heaven is overhead.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaven is traditionally placed up in the sky, so being there means being overhead, on high.

clue.text: See 15
See 19
Mouse taken from sucker?

definitions.note: a phrase for what is taken, not a noun synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: the Disney cartoon mouse
second meaning: what you take out of a dupe when you mock him

explanation.walkthrough: To take the mickey out of someone is British slang for teasing or mocking them, and a sucker is the obvious target.
explanation.definitionFit: Disney's famous cartoon rodent shares his first name with the thing taken in the idiom for ridiculing a person.

clue.text: Throne for two to carry one, a job at Cambridge or London?

definitions.text: Throne for two to carry one
a job at Cambridge or London?

blocks.clueFragment: Throne for two to carry one
blocks.note: first meaning: the seat two people make by gripping each other's wrists to carry a third

blocks.clueFragment: a job at Cambridge or London?
blocks.note: second meaning: a professorship at King's College, which exists in both universities

explanation.walkthrough: King's College is a college of both Cambridge and London universities, and a chair is a professorship.
explanation.definitionFit: The children's carrying seat made of four clasped hands is so named, and an academic chair at King's would be a post there.

clue.text: Intrepid nobleman in heraldic band

indicators.note: in places the nobleman within the heraldic band, which surrounds him

blocks.note: a fess is a broad horizontal band across a coat of arms
an earl is a British nobleman

explanation.surface: A brave aristocrat is pictured on a stripe of his family's coat of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: Heraldry has its own vocabulary: the fess is one of the basic bands, alongside the bend and the pale.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone intrepid shows no fear at all, so the two adjectives are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: ?19 25 11 maybe hamper 7 of 9, according to the old song (how many times?)

definitions.text: ?19 25 11 maybe hamper 7 of 9, according to the old song (how many times?)

blocks.note: surface: a jumble of cross-references about rain and things falling from the sky

blocks.clueFragment: according to the old song (how many times?)
blocks.note: setter's reading: the 1936 song says that every time it rains this is what comes down

explanation.walkthrough: The Bing Crosby song runs 'Every time it rains, it rains pennies from heaven'; '(how many times?)' prompts 'every time', and the cross-references play on the rain proverb at 19.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the old popular song names the windfall that falls with the rain, an unexpected gift of money.

clue.text: Spiritual chucker out to be detaining a killer

indicators.note: to detain is to hold, so the verb holds the killer inside it

blocks.note: to exist is to be
an orc is a killer whale

explanation.surface: A bouncer of the soul is about to arrest a murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: EX(ORC)IST. 'Chucker out' is British slang for a bouncer.
explanation.definitionFit: An exorcist drives evil spirits out of a person or place, so is a bouncer for the spirit world.

clue.text: See 26
Want fish? There's some provocation

blocks.note: to want is to need
the ling is a long cod-like sea fish

explanation.surface: A hungry person asking for fish is accused of stirring up trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Needling is persistent teasing or goading meant to irritate, so it counts as provocation.

clue.text: There's perpetual drought, product of 20 pi - it's not "the gentle ... 10 22across"

annotation.answer: IT NEVER RAINS BUT IT POURS

definitions.text: There's perpetual drought, product of 20 pi - it's not "the gentle ... 10 22across"

blocks.note: first half of the saying read literally: no rain ever falls

blocks.clueFragment: product of 20 pi - it's not "the gentle ... 10 22across"
blocks.note: second half: what comes from a burst pipe is a torrent, not Portia's gentle rain from heaven

explanation.walkthrough: 20 is BURST OUT, so '20 pi' hints at a burst pipe, which pours. Portia's speech in The Merchant of Venice has mercy dropping 'as the gentle rain from heaven'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says misfortunes never come singly, built from a joke about drought giving way to a deluge.

clue.text: See 17
Turn and learn with turn of a wrist bone

indicators.note: the word learn comes with a turn, so its letters are twisted round into another order

blocks.note: a U-turn, so U stands for a turn
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to rotate and study the movement of a joint in the hand.
explanation.walkthrough: U then LEARN rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulnare is the carpal bone on the ulna side of the wrist, also called the triquetral or cuneiform bone.

clue.text: See 15
Take place, maybe, in Lancashire?

definitions.note: an adverb in dialect, unlike the verb

blocks.note: first meaning: to occur
second meaning: in northern English dialect the word means perhaps, usually said without its H

explanation.walkthrough: In Lancashire and Yorkshire dialect ''appen' is used for 'perhaps', as in ''appen it'll rain'.
explanation.definitionFit: To happen is to occur or come about, and northern speech also uses the same word as an adverb meaning perhaps.

clue.text: Economically - maybe not he - he's into the top limit

indicators.note: maybe hints that the words can be taken as a possible rearrangement rather than as they stand
going into something puts it inside, so the pronoun sits within the limit

blocks.note: taken as written
a cap is an upper limit, as on spending
taken as written

explanation.surface: A thrifty man is pushed up against the spending ceiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe not he' reads like a hedge about some person, but it is the fodder with its anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on the cheap means doing it for as little money as possible, frugally.

clue.text: Dweller in 22 across holds a pound, not 15

definitions.note: a contrast: the precious metal as opposed to copper coins

indicators.note: the dweller holds the pound, keeping it within himself

blocks.note: 22 across is heaven, where God lives
L, from Latin libra, is the pound sign

explanation.surface: The resident of heaven keeps hold of a pound, not mere pennies.
explanation.walkthrough: GO(L)D. 15 is PENNIES FROM HEAVEN, so the definition asks for a metal other than the copper of pennies.
explanation.definitionFit: Pennies are copper coins, so gold is the precious metal at the opposite end of the coinage scale.

clue.text: Hospital people in demand for 15?

blocks.note: first meaning: a well-known teaching hospital in London
second meaning: the effigies children display on Bonfire Night, begging 'a penny for the guy'

explanation.walkthrough: Guy's is a London hospital. Before 5 November British children wheel round a stuffed figure of Guy Fawkes asking passers-by for a penny for the guy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bonfire Night effigies are called guys and are used to beg for coins, and the hospital bears the same name.

clue.text: See 19
All Lundy editor's work - stickers, all French, on wrong piece of gingerbread: they were winged (Sassoon)

indicators.note: the editor's work on a text reshapes it, so these letters are reworked
only a piece of the cake is wanted, so its tail is cut away

blocks.note: all people means everyone
taken as written; Lundy is an island in the Bristol Channel
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor, plus the S
burs are prickly seed heads that stick to clothing
tout is French for all
a sin is a wrong
taken as written, before trimming

explanation.surface: A bewildering list of an island editor, burrs and gingerbread, closed by a nod to a war poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Siegfried Sassoon's 1919 poem, in which 'Everyone was a bird', hence they were winged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassoon's poem compares the joyful singers to caged birds set free, so its title describes people given wings.
